Suffridge’s Convolution Theorem for Polynomials and Entire Functions Having Only Real ZerosThanks: Most of the research that led to this paper was conducted while I had a post-doc position at the math department of the University of Würzburg. I am very grateful to Stephan Ruscheweyh and all members of Lehrstuhl IV for the productive and friendly atmosphere there.

Martin Lamprecht Address: Department of Computer Science and Engineering
School of Sciences
European University of Cyprus
Diogenous Str. 6, Engomi, P.O. Box: 22006, 1516 Nicosia, Cyprus Email address: m.lamprecht@euc.ac.cy
Abstract.

We present a Suffridge-like extension of the Grace-Szegö convolution theorem for polynomials and entire functions with only real zeros. Our results can also be seen as a qq-extension of Pólya’s and Schur’s characterization of multiplier sequences. As a limit case we obtain a new characterization of all log-concave sequences in terms of the zero location of certain associated polynomials. Our results also lead to an extension of Ruscheweyh’s convolution lemma for functions which are analytic in the unit disk and to new necessary conditions for the validity of the Riemann Conjecture.

Key words and phrases: 
Suffridge polynomials, Pólya-Schur multiplier sequences, qq-binomials, log-concave sequences, Newton’s inequalities, Ruscheweyh convolution lemma, Riemann Conjecture
2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
30C10, 30C15, 26C10, 30D15, 05A99, 11M26

1. Introduction

In [21] Rota states: “Grace’s theorem is an instance of what might be called a sturdy theorem. For almost one hundred years it has resisted all attempts at generalization. Almost all known results about the distribution of zeros of polynomials in the complex plane are corollaries of Grace’s theorem.”

The following equivalent formulation of Grace’s theorem is due to Szegö.

Theorem 1 (Grace [11], Szegö [33]).

Let

F⁡(z)=∑k=0n(nk)​ak​zkandG⁡(z)=∑k=0n(nk)​bk​zkF(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}{n\choose k}a_{k}z^{k}\quad\mbox{and}\quad G(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}{n\choose k}b_{k}z^{k}

be polynomials of degree n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} and suppose K⊂ℂK\subset\mathbb{C} is an open or closed disk or half-plane, or the open or closed exterior of a disk, that contains all zeros of FF. If G⁡(0)≠0G(0)\neq 0, then each zero γ\gamma of

F∗G​SG⁡(z):=∑k=0n(nk)​ak​bk​zkF*_{GS}G(z):=\sum_{k=0}^{n}{n\choose k}a_{k}b_{k}z^{k}

is of the form γ=−α​β\gamma=-\alpha\beta with α∈K\alpha\in K and G⁡(β)=0G(\beta)=0. If G⁡(0)=0G(0)=0, then this continues to hold as long as KK is not the open or closed exterior of a disk.

Rota is right (of course): This theorem includes or implies most other known results concerning the zero location of complex polynomials. It has found numerous applications in complex analysis and other fields. For instance, it forms the basis of the geometric convolution theory which was developed by Ruscheweyh, Suffridge, and Sheil-Small (see [23, 24, 28, 29, 30, 32] and, more recently, [25, 26, 27]) and it can be used to classify all linear operators which preserve the set of polynomials whose zeros lie in a given circular domain (cf. [24, Thm. 1.1], [30, Sec. 5.8], and [4]). Very recently, in an impressive series of papers [2, 3, 5], Borcea and Bränden used Grace’s theorem in order to develop a unified analytic theory of multivariate polynomials with many astonishing applications.

In this paper we will present a real polynomial analogue of a striking extension of the Grace-Szegö convolution theorem which was found by Suffridge in [32]. Our result can also be seen as a qq-extension and a finite difference analogue [6] of Pólya’s and Schur’s [19] famous classification of multiplier sequences. As consequences we obtain a new classification of all log-concave sequences in terms of the zero location of certain associated polynomials, several analogues of a convolution lemma of Ruscheweyh which is of great importance in the convolution theory of functions analytic in 𝔻\mathbb{D}, and a new continuous connection between the Riemann Conjecture and a necessary condition of it which was verified by Csordas, Norfolk, and Varga in [8].

We believe that Suffridge’s work [32], the recent work of Ruscheweyh and Salinas [25, 26, 27], and the results of this paper and [13] (the methods of proof presented here and in [13] also seem to have some kind of resemblance to the methods used in [10]), strongly hint at a very deep lying extension of Grace’s theorem which will lead to a much better understanding of the relation between the zeros and the coefficients of complex polynomials.

1.1. Special cases of the Grace-Szegö convolution theorem

As usual, for a field 𝕂\mathbb{K} we denote the set of polynomials of degree ≤n\leq n (this includes the polynomial identically 00 which is of degree −1-1) over 𝕂\mathbb{K} by 𝕂n​[z]\mathbb{K}_{n}[z] (the only fields 𝕂\mathbb{K} that will be considered in this paper are ℂ\mathbb{C} and ℝ\mathbb{R}). 𝕂⁡[z]\mathbb{K}[z] denotes the set of all polynomials over 𝕂\mathbb{K} and 𝕂⁡[[z]]\mathbb{K}[[z]] is the set of formal power series over 𝕂\mathbb{K}. If f∈𝕂⁡[[z]]∖𝕂⁡[z]f\in\mathbb{K}[[z]]\setminus\mathbb{K}[z], then we set deg⁡f:=+∞\deg f:=+\infty. The convolution or Hadamard product of f⁡(z)=∑k=0∞ak​zkf(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_{k}z^{k}, g⁡(z)=∑k=0∞bk​zk∈ℂ⁡[[z]]g(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}b_{k}z^{k}\in\mathbb{C}[[z]] is defined by

f∗g⁡(z)=∑k=0∞ak​bk​zk.f*g(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_{k}b_{k}z^{k}.

The multiplier class ℳ⁡(𝒳)\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{X}) of a subset 𝒳\mathcal{X} of ℂ⁡[[z]]\mathbb{C}[[z]] consists of those g∈ℂ⁡[[z]]g\in\mathbb{C}[[z]] with deg⁡g≤max⁡{deg⁡h:h∈𝒳}\deg g\leq\max\{\deg h:h\in\mathcal{X}\} which have the property that f∗g∈𝒳f*g\in\mathcal{X} for all f∈𝒳f\in\mathcal{X}.

For an unbounded subset Ω\Omega of ℂ\mathbb{C} we define πn​(Ω)\pi_{n}(\Omega) to be the set of all polynomials in ℂn​[z]\mathbb{C}_{n}[z] which have zeros only in Ω\Omega. If Ω\Omega is bounded, then πn​(Ω)\pi_{n}(\Omega) shall contain all polynomials of degree nn with zeros only in Ω\Omega. For every Ω⊂ℂ\Omega\subset\mathbb{C} the class πn​(Ω)\pi_{n}(\Omega) shall also contain the polynomial identically zero. σn​(Ω)\sigma_{n}(\Omega) will denote the union of {0}\{0\} with the set of all polynomials in πn​(Ω)\pi_{n}(\Omega) which have only simple zeros and which, in the case that Ω\Omega is unbounded, are of degree nn or n−1n-1. Finally, for 𝒳⊂ℂ⁡[[z]]\mathcal{X}\subset\mathbb{C}[[z]] and h∈ℂ⁡[[z]]h\in\mathbb{C}[[z]] we denote by 𝒫⁡(𝒳,h)\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X};h) the pre-coefficient class of 𝒳\mathcal{X} with respect to hh, i.e. those f∈ℂ⁡[[z]]f\in\mathbb{C}[[z]] with deg⁡f≤deg⁡h\deg f\leq\deg h for which f∗h∈𝒳f*h\in\mathcal{X}.

Several interesting special cases of the Grace-Szegö convolution theorem can now be stated as follows (for a detailed proof see [20, Ch. 5]). 1.2. Suffridge’s extension of the unit circle case

Evidently, the binomial coefficients and their generating polynomial

(1+z)n=∑k=0n(nk)​zk(1+z)^{n}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}{n\choose k}z^{k}

play an essential role in the Grace-Szegö convolution theorem. A particularly interesting extension of the binomial coefficients are the qq-binomial or Gaussian binomial coefficients Ckn​(q)C_{k}^{n}(q) which are defined by

(1) Rn​(q,z):=∑k=0nCkn​(q)​zk:=∏j=1n(1+qj−1​z),q∈ℂ,R_{n}(q;z):=\sum_{k=0}^{n}C_{k}^{n}(q)z^{k}:=\prod_{j=1}^{n}(1+q^{j-1}z),\qquad q\in\mathbb{C},

and take the explicit form [1, (10.0.5)]

(2) Ckn​(q)=qk⁡(k−1)/2​∏j=1k1−qj+n−k1−qj,k∈{0,…,n}.C_{k}^{n}(q)=q^{k(k-1)/2}\prod_{j=1}^{k}\frac{1-q^{j+n-k}}{1-q^{j}},\quad k\in\{0,\ldots,n\}.

Observe that often (for instance in [1]) q−k(k−1)/2Ckn(q)q^{-k(k-1)/2}C_{k}^{n}(q) are defined to be the qq-binomial coefficients. If q∈𝕋q\in\mathbb{T}, then all zeros of Rn​(q,z)R_{n}(q;z) lie on the unit circle and are separated by a certain angle. In [32] Suffridge considered subclasses of πn​(𝕋)\pi_{n}(\mathbb{T}) in which Rn​(ei​λ,z)R_{n}(e^{i\lambda};z), with λ∈[0,2​πn]\lambda\in[0,\frac{2\pi}{n}], is an extremal element.

In order to be more exact, for n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} and λ∈[0,2​πn]\lambda\in[0,\frac{2\pi}{n}] we define the classes 𝒯n​(λ)\mathcal{T}_{n}(\lambda) to consist of all polynomials F∈πn​(𝕋)F\in\pi_{n}(\mathbb{T}) which have the property that if z1z_{1}, z2∈𝕋z_{2}\in\mathbb{T} are zeros of FF (the zeros, as always in this paper, counted according to multiplicity), then z1z_{1} and z2z_{2} are separated by an angle >λ>\lambda. We also define 00 to be an element of 𝒯n​(λ)\mathcal{T}_{n}(\lambda). The closure 𝒯¯n​(λ)\overline{\mathcal{T}}_{n}(\lambda) of 𝒯n​(λ)\mathcal{T}_{n}(\lambda) then contains 00 and all polynomials in πn​(𝕋)\pi_{n}(\mathbb{T}) whose zeros are separated by an angle ≥λ\geq\lambda. The classes 𝒯¯n​(λ)\overline{\mathcal{T}}_{n}(\lambda) were introduced by Suffridge in [32] (where they were denoted by 𝒫n​(λ)\mathcal{P}_{n}(\lambda), however, and did not contain 00).

Every pair (except one) of successive zeros of

(3) Qn(λ;z):=∏j=1n(1+ei⁡(2​j−n−1)​λ/2z)=Rn(ei​λ;e−i(n−1)λ/2z)Q_{n}(\lambda;z):=\prod_{j=1}^{n}(1+e^{i(2j-n-1)\lambda/2}z)=R_{n}(e^{i\lambda};e^{-i(n-1)\lambda/2}z)

is separated by an angle of exactly λ\lambda. This is the reason why, as indicated above, we call a polynomial FF in 𝒯¯n​(λ)\overline{\mathcal{T}}_{n}(\lambda) extremal if there is an a∈𝕋a\in\mathbb{T} such that F(z)=ℂQn(λ;az)F(z)=_{\mathbb{C}}Q_{n}(\lambda;az), where, from now on, for FF, G∈ℂ⁡[[z]]G\in\mathbb{C}[[z]] and 𝕂=ℝ\mathbb{K}=\mathbb{R} or 𝕂=ℂ\mathbb{K}=\mathbb{C} we write F=𝕂GF=_{\mathbb{K}}G if there is an a∈𝕂∖{0}a\in\mathbb{K}\setminus\{0\} such that F=a​GF=aG. For λ∈[0,2​πn)\lambda\in[0,\frac{2\pi}{n}) we set 𝒫​𝒯n​(λ):=𝒫⁡(𝒯n​(λ),Qn​(λ,z))\mathcal{PT}_{n}(\lambda):=\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{T}_{n}(\lambda);Q_{n}(\lambda;z)), while

𝒫​𝒯n​(2​πn):=⋃λ∈[0,2​πn)𝒫​𝒯n​(λ).\mathcal{PT}_{n}\left(\frac{2\pi}{n}\right):=\bigcup_{\lambda\in[0,\frac{2\pi}{n})}\mathcal{PT}_{n}(\lambda).

We call a polynomial f∈𝒫​𝒯¯n​(λ)f\in\overline{\mathcal{PT}}_{n}(\lambda) extremal if f∗Qn​(λ,z)f*Q_{n}(\lambda;z) is extremal in 𝒯¯n​(λ)\overline{\mathcal{T}}_{n}(\lambda), i.e. if there is an a∈𝕋a\in\mathbb{T} such that f(z)=ℂen(az)f(z)=_{\mathbb{C}}e_{n}(az) with

en​(z)=1+z+⋯+zn−1+zn.e_{n}(z)=1+z+\cdots+z^{n-1}+z^{n}.

Suffridge’s stunning results from [32] now read as follows.

Theorem 3 (Suffridge).

Let λ∈[0,2​πn]\lambda\in[0,\frac{2\pi}{n}].

  1. (a)

    We have ℳ⁡(𝒫​𝒯n​(λ))=𝒫​𝒯¯n​(λ)\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{PT}_{n}(\lambda))=\overline{\mathcal{PT}}_{n}(\lambda). In particular, for λ∈[0,2​πn)\lambda\in[0,\frac{2\pi}{n}) we have ℳ⁡(𝒯n​(λ))=𝒫​𝒯¯n​(λ)\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{T}_{n}(\lambda))=\overline{\mathcal{PT}}_{n}(\lambda).

  2. (b)

    If μ∈(λ,2​πn]\mu\in(\lambda,\frac{2\pi}{n}] and f∈𝒫​𝒯¯n​(λ)f\in\overline{\mathcal{PT}}_{n}(\lambda) is not extremal, then f∈𝒫​𝒯n​(μ)f\in\mathcal{PT}_{n}(\mu).

  3. (c)

    We have

    𝒫​𝒯¯n(2​πn)=⋃a∈𝕋,b∈ℂco{ben(e2​i​j​π/naz):j=1,…,n},\overline{\mathcal{PT}}_{n}\left(\frac{2\pi}{n}\right)=\bigcup_{a\in\mathbb{T},b\in\mathbb{C}}\operatorname{co}\{b\,e_{n}(e^{2ij\pi/n}az):j=1,\ldots,n\},

    where co⁡M\operatorname{co}M denotes the convex hull of a subset MM of a complex vector space.

Since 𝒯¯n​(0)=πn​(𝕋)\overline{\mathcal{T}}_{n}(0)=\pi_{n}(\mathbb{T}), 𝒯n​(0)=σn​(𝕋)⊂πn​(𝕋)\mathcal{T}_{n}(0)=\sigma_{n}(\mathbb{T})\subset\pi_{n}(\mathbb{T}), and Qn​(0,z)=(1+z)nQ_{n}(0;z)=(1+z)^{n}, (1) and (3) show that Theorem 3(a) can be seen as a qq-extension of Corollary 2(b).

Naturally, this extension of Corollary 2(b) triggers the question whether there are other statements of Corollary 2 that can be generalized in a similar way. In this paper we will show how to obtain qq-extensions (for real qq) of Statements (c)–(e) of Corollary 2(b) by modifying the proof of Suffridge’s theorem that is given in [13].

2. Main results

2.1. Suffridge’s theorem for real polynomials

The main idea for obtaining a real polynomial version of Suffridge’s theorem is to consider Rn​(q,z)R_{n}(q;z) with q∈[0,1]q\in[0,1] as an extremal polynomial for certain classes of real polynomials.

Recall that

Rn​(q,z)=∑k=0nCkn​(q)​zk=∏j=1n(1+qj−1​z),n∈ℕ,q∈[0,1].R_{n}(q;z)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}C_{k}^{n}(q)z^{k}=\prod_{j=1}^{n}(1+q^{j-1}z),\qquad n\in\mathbb{N},\;q\in[0,1].

Hence, for q∈(0,1]q\in(0,1] the zeros xj:=−q−jx_{j}:=-q^{-j}, j∈{0,…,n−1}j\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}, of Rn​(q,z)R_{n}(q;z) satisfy the separation condition xj/xk≤qx_{j}/x_{k}\leq q for k>jk>j. If we suppose Rn​(q,z)R_{n}(q;z) to be extremal for a certain class of real polynomials, we are therefore led to the following definitions.

For q∈[0,1]q\in[0,1] we call a finite or infinite sequence {xk}k\{x_{k}\}_{k} of real numbers logarithmically qq-separated, or shorter qq-separated, if xk/xl≤qx_{k}/x_{l}\leq q for all indices kk, ll with k≠lk\neq l for which either xl≤xk<0x_{l}\leq x_{k}<0 or 0<xk≤xl0<x_{k}\leq x_{l} holds. If xk/xl<qx_{k}/x_{l}<q for all such indices kk, ll, then {xk}k\{x_{k}\}_{k} is called strictly logarithmically qq-separated, or strictly qq-separated. For n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} and q∈[0,1]q\in[0,1] we define ℛn​(q)\mathcal{R}_{n}(q) as the union of {0}\{0\} with the set of real polynomials in πn​(ℝ)\pi_{n}(\mathbb{R}) that have strictly qq-separated zeros. 𝒩n​(q)\mathcal{N}_{n}(q) will denote ℛn​(q)∩πn​(ℝ0−)\mathcal{R}_{n}(q)\cap\pi_{n}(\mathbb{R}^{-}_{0}). Rn​(q,z)R_{n}(q;z) belongs to both ℛ¯n​(q)\overline{\mathcal{R}}_{n}(q) and 𝒩¯n​(q)\overline{\mathcal{N}}_{n}(q), and we call a polynomial FF in one of these two classes extremal if there is an a∈ℝ∖{0}a\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\} such that F(z)=ℝRn(q;az)F(z)=_{\mathbb{R}}R_{n}(q;az). For q∈(0,1]q\in(0,1] we further set 𝒫​ℛn​(q):=𝒫⁡(ℛn​(q),Rn​(q,z))\mathcal{PR}_{n}(q):=\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{R}_{n}(q);R_{n}(q;z)), 𝒫​𝒩n​(q):=𝒫⁡(𝒩n​(q),Rn​(q,z))\mathcal{PN}_{n}(q):=\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{N}_{n}(q);R_{n}(q;z)),

𝒫​ℛn​(0):=⋃q∈(0,1]𝒫​ℛn​(q)and𝒫​𝒩n​(0):=⋃q∈(0,1]𝒫​𝒩n​(q).\mathcal{PR}_{n}(0):=\bigcup_{q\in(0,1]}\mathcal{PR}_{n}(q)\quad\mbox{and}\quad\mathcal{PN}_{n}(0):=\bigcup_{q\in(0,1]}\mathcal{PN}_{n}(q).

Theorem 4.

Let q∈[0,1]q\in[0,1] and n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}.

    We have

    𝒫​ℛn​(0)=ℒ​𝒞nand𝒫​𝒩n​(0)=ℒ​𝒞n+.\mathcal{PR}_{n}(0)=\mathcal{LC}_{n}\quad\mbox{and}\quad\mathcal{PN}_{n}(0)=\mathcal{LC}_{n}^{+}.

Statements (a)–(c) of this theorem are obtained as corollaries of certain interspersion invariance results concerning the classes ℛ¯n​(q)\overline{\mathcal{R}}_{n}(q) and 𝒩¯n​(q)\overline{\mathcal{N}}_{n}(q) (Theorems 29 and 30). Together with the Hermite-Biehler theorem (cf. [20, Thm. 6.3.4]), these results also lead to a qq-extension of Corollary 2(c) (Theorem 33). Details will be given in Section 7.

The cases q=1q=1 of Theorem 4(a) and Theorem 5(a) were first obtained by Pólya and Schur in [19] and they called them, respectively, the algebraic characterization of multiplier sequences of the first kind and the transcendental characterization of these sequences. Theorems 4(a) and 5(a) thus represent a qq-extension and a finite difference analogue (cf. [6]) of Pólya’s and Schur’s characterization of multiplier sequences.

Note also that, as a limit case of Theorem 3, in [32], Suffridge obtained a second proof (the first one was given by by Ruscheweyh and Sheil-Small [28], see also [15, 24, 30]) of a conjecture of Pólya and Schoenberg from [18] which claimed that the convolution of two convex univalent function is again convex univalent. Statements (a) and (b) of Theorem 5 can thus also be seen as the real entire function analogues of the Pólya-Schoenberg conjecture.

2.3. A new characterization of log-concave sequences

Log-concave sequences play an important role in combinatorics, algebra, geometry, computer science, probability, and statistics (see [7, 31]), and therefore Theorems 4(d) and 5(d) might have far-reaching applications. An important tool for establishing the log-concavity of a given sequence {ak}k\{a_{k}\}_{k} of real numbers are ”Newton’s inequalities” (see [31, Thm. 2]), which state that {ak}k=0n\{a_{k}\}_{k=0}^{n}, n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, is log-concave, if ∑k=0n(nk)​ak​zk\sum_{k=0}^{n}{n\choose k}a_{k}z^{k} is a real polynomial with only real zeros. This sufficient condition for log-concavity is however far from necessary.

As a corollary to Theorems 4(d) and 5(d) we obtain the following new characterization of all log-concave sequences in terms of the zero location of certain associated polynomials.

Corollary 6.

Let n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} and suppose {ak}k=0n\{a_{k}\}_{k=0}^{n} is a sequence of real numbers. Then {ak}k=0n\{a_{k}\}_{k=0}^{n} is strictly log-concave if, and only if, there is a q∈(0,1]q\in(0,1] such that

∑k=0nCkn​(q)​ak​zkbelongs toℛn​(q).\sum_{k=0}^{n}C_{k}^{n}(q)a_{k}z^{k}\quad\mbox{belongs to}\quad\mathcal{R}_{n}(q).

If all aka_{k} are non-negative, then ∑k=0nCkn​(q)​ak​zk\sum_{k=0}^{n}C_{k}^{n}(q)a_{k}z^{k} belongs to 𝒩n​(q)\mathcal{N}_{n}(q).

Moreover, if there is a q∈(0,1]q\in(0,1] and an infinite sequence {ak}k=0∞\{a_{k}\}_{k=0}^{\infty} of real numbers such that

∑k=0∞Ck∞​(q)​ak​zkbelongs toℛ¯∞​(q),\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}C_{k}^{\infty}(q)a_{k}z^{k}\quad\mbox{belongs to}\quad\overline{\mathcal{R}}_{\infty}(q),

then {ak}k=0∞\{a_{k}\}_{k=0}^{\infty} is strictly log-concave.

Using the Hermite-Biehler theorem [20, Thm. 6.3.4] and Lemma 23, one sees that in order to verify whether a given sequence {ak}k=0n\{a_{k}\}_{k=0}^{n} is strictly log-concave it is also sufficient to check whether all zeros ≠0\neq 0 of the polynomial

∑k=0n(Ckn​(q)​ak+i​qk−1​Ck−1n​(q)​ak−1)​zk\sum_{k=0}^{n}\left(C_{k}^{n}(q)a_{k}+iq^{k-1}C_{k-1}^{n}(q)a_{k-1}\right)z^{k}

lie in the open upper half-plane 𝕌\mathbb{U} or in the open lower half-plane 𝕃\mathbb{L} (if ak≥0a_{k}\geq 0 for all k∈{0,…,n}k\in\{0,\ldots,n\} it is even enough to check whether all zeros ≠0\neq 0 of the polynomial ∑k=0nCkn​(q)​ak​(1+i​qk)​zk\sum_{k=0}^{n}C_{k}^{n}(q)a_{k}\left(1+iq^{k}\right)z^{k} lie in 𝕌\mathbb{U} or 𝕃\mathbb{L}).

2.4. An extension of Ruscheweh’s convolution lemma

The following lemma of Ruscheweyh from [22] plays a fundamental role in the convolution theory for functions which are analytic in 𝔻\mathbb{D} (see [24]). ℋ⁡(𝔻)\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D}) denotes the set of functions analytic in 𝔻\mathbb{D} and ℋ0​(𝔻)\mathcal{H}_{0}(\mathbb{D}) is the set of those functions f∈ℋ⁡(𝔻)f\in\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D}) which satisfy f⁡(0)=f′​(0)−1=0f(0)=f^{\prime}(0)-1=0.

Lemma 7 (Ruscheweyh).

Suppose ff, g∈ℋ0​(𝔻)g\in\mathcal{H}_{0}(\mathbb{D}) satisfy

(f∗1+x​z1+y​z​g)​(z)≠0for allz∈𝔻,x,y∈𝕋.\left(f*\frac{1+xz}{1+yz}g\right)(z)\neq 0\quad\mbox{for all}\quad z\in\mathbb{D},\;x,y\in\mathbb{T}.

Then for every g∈ℋ⁡(𝔻)g\in\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D}) we have

f∗hf∗g​(𝔻)⊂co¯​(hg​(𝔻)).\frac{f*h}{f*g}(\mathbb{D})\subset\overline{\operatorname{co}}\left(\frac{h}{g}(\mathbb{D})\right).

Let L:ℋ⁡(𝔻)→ℋ⁡(𝔻)L:\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D})\rightarrow\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D}) be a continuous complex linear operator. Suppose f∈ℋ⁡(𝔻)f\in\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D}) is such that

and

Then for every g∈ℋ⁡(𝔻)g\in\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D}) we have

2.5. Consequences regarding the Riemann Conjecture

It is well known (and explained in [8], for example) that the Riemann Conjecture is equivalent to the statement that

F⁡(z)=∑n=0∞b^n​zn(2​n)!F(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{\hat{b}_{n}z^{n}}{(2n)!}

belongs to 𝒩¯∞​(1)\overline{\mathcal{N}}_{\infty}(1), where

b^n:=∫0∞t2​nΦ(t)dt,n∈ℕ0,andΦ(t):=∑n=1∞(2n4π2e9​t−3n2πe5​t)e−n2​π​e4​t.\hat{b}_{n}:=\int_{0}^{\infty}t^{2n}\Phi(t)\,dt,\quad n\in\mathbb{N}_{0},\quad\mbox{and}\quad\Phi(t):=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(2n^{4}\pi^{2}e^{9t}-3n^{2}\pi e^{5t})e^{-n^{2}\pi e^{4t}}.

A particular consequence of Theorem 5 concerning the Riemann Conjecture is the following.

Theorem 9.

If the Riemann Conjecture is true, then

f⁡(z)=∑n=0∞n!​b^n​zn(2​n)!∈𝒫​𝒩¯∞​(q)⊂ℒ​𝒞+¯∞for allq∈(0,1].f(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{n!\hat{b}_{n}z^{n}}{(2n)!}\in\overline{\mathcal{PN}}_{\infty}(q)\subset\overline{\mathcal{LC}^{+}}_{\infty}\quad\mbox{for all}\quad q\in(0,1].

The statement f∈𝒫​𝒩¯∞​(q)f\in\overline{\mathcal{PN}}_{\infty}(q) is a necessary condition for the validity of the Riemann Conjecture, that becomes weaker as qq decreases from 11 to 00. Its weakest form (f∈ℒ​𝒞+¯∞f\in\overline{\mathcal{LC}^{+}}_{\infty}) is true due to Csordas, Norfolk, and Varga [8].

2.6. Structure of the paper

In the next section we introduce some terminology and notation regarding zeros and poles of polynomials and rational functions. In Section 4 we establish certain facts regarding polynomials with interspersed zeros, and obtain, as main result, Lemma 16 (the real polynomial version of Ruscheweyh’s convolution lemma). In Section 5 we prove certain analogues of results from Section 4 for polynomials with log-interspersed zeros. The main result, Lemma 22, is also an analogue of Ruscheweyh’s convolution lemma. In Section 6 several auxiliary results concerning the classes ℛ¯n​(q)\overline{\mathcal{R}}_{n}(q) and 𝒩¯n​(q)\overline{\mathcal{N}}_{n}(q) are verified, among them a qq-extension of Newton’s inequalities (Theorem 27) and qq-extensions of the theorems of Rolle (Theorem 25) and Laguerre (Theorem 28). In Section 6 we prove Theorem 4 and a qq-extension of Corollary 2(c) by means of two interspersion invariance results (Theorems 29 and 30) concerning the classes ℛ¯n​(q)\overline{\mathcal{R}}_{n}(q) and 𝒩¯n​(q)\overline{\mathcal{N}}_{n}(q), which are of independent interest. In the final Section 8 we present the proof of Lemma 8.

3. Zeros and nn-Zeros of Polynomials and Rational Functions

We consider ℝ¯:=ℝ∪{∞}\overline{\mathbb{R}}:=\mathbb{R}\cup\{\infty\} as being diffeomorphic to the unit circle 𝕋:={z∈ℂ:|z|=1}\mathbb{T}:=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|=1\} in the Riemann sphere ℂ¯:=ℂ∪{∞}\overline{\mathbb{C}}:=\mathbb{C}\cup\{\infty\}. In that spirit, we use the convention ±∞:=∞\pm\infty:=\infty in expressions like (a,+∞](a,+\infty] with a∈ℝa\in\mathbb{R}, i.e. if b∈(a,+∞]b\in(a,+\infty] and bb is not finite then b=∞b=\infty.

A function FF that is analytic in a neighborhood of z∈ℂz\in\mathbb{C} has a zero of order (or multiplicity) m∈ℕ0m\in\mathbb{N}_{0} at zz if F(k)​(z)=0F^{(k)}(z)=0 for k∈{0,…,m−1}k\in\{0,\ldots,m-1\} and F(m)​(z)≠0F^{(m)}(z)\neq 0. ord⁡(F,z)\operatorname{ord}(F;z) will denote the order of z∈ℂz\in\mathbb{C} as a zero of FF. For a polynomial FF of degree ≤n\leq n we set

(8) F∗n​(z):=zn​F​(−1z).F^{*n}(z):=z^{n}F\left(-\frac{1}{z}\right).

In this way the number of nn-zeros of every polynomial FF of degree m∈{0,1,…,n}m\in\{0,1,\ldots,n\} is exactly nn (counted according to multiplicity), since such a polynomial has an nn-zero of order n−mn-m at ∞\infty.

A rational function RR is of degree n∈ℕ0n\in\mathbb{N}_{0} if R=F/GR=F/G with polynomials F⁡(z)=an​zn+⋯+a0​\nequiv​0F(z)=a_{n}z^{n}+\cdots+a_{0}\nequiv 0 and G⁡(z)=bn​zn+⋯+b0​\nequiv​0G(z)=b_{n}z^{n}+\cdots+b_{0}\nequiv 0 that have no common zeros and for which n=max⁡{deg⁡F,deg⁡G}n=\max\{\deg F,\deg G\}. We extend RR to ℂ¯\overline{\mathbb{C}} by letting R⁡(∞)R(\infty) be equal to an/bna_{n}/b_{n} or ∞\infty depending on whether bn≠0b_{n}\neq 0 or bn=0b_{n}=0. If R⁡(∞)=0R(\infty)=0, then the order of the zero ∞\infty of RR is defined to be the order of the zero of R(−1/z)R(-1/z) at the origin (i.e. ord(R;∞):=ord(R(−1/z);0)\operatorname{ord}(R;\infty):=\operatorname{ord}(R(-1/z);0)). If RR is a rational function for which R⁡(∞)R(\infty) is finite, then we set R′​(∞):=(R∘ψ)′​(0)R^{\prime}(\infty):=(R\circ\psi)^{\prime}(0), where ψ(z):=−1/z\psi(z):=-1/z. One can then see that if a rational function RR has a pole of order ≥2\geq 2 or a local extremum at z∈ℝ¯z\in\overline{\mathbb{R}}, then R′​(z)=0R^{\prime}(z)=0, and that if R′​(z)≠0R^{\prime}(z)\neq 0, then there is a neighborhood U⊂ℝ¯U\subset\overline{\mathbb{R}} of zz such that R′​(w)​R′​(z)>0R^{\prime}(w)R^{\prime}(z)>0 for all w∈Uw\in U.

4. Linear Operators Preserving Interspersion

We say that two polynomials FF, G∈ℝ⁡[z]G\in\mathbb{R}[z] with only real zeros have interspersed zeros if between every pair of successive zeros of FF there is exactly one zero of GG (the zeros counted according to multiplicity). Moreover, we will use the convention that every polynomial F∈ℝ⁡[z]F\in\mathbb{R}[z] with only real zeros and the polynomial 00 have interspersed zeros. A particular consequence of this definition is the following.

Lemma 10.

If FF, G∈ℝn​[z]∖{0}G\in\mathbb{R}_{n}[z]\setminus\{0\} have interspersed zeros and if x∈ℝ¯x\in\overline{\mathbb{R}} is an nn-zero of order mm of FF, then ordn⁡(G;x)∈{m−1,m,m+1}\operatorname{ord}_{n}(G;x)\in\{m-1,m,m+1\}. In particular, if FF and GG have interspersed zeros, then |deg⁡F−deg⁡G|≤1|\deg F-\deg G|\leq 1.

If FF, G∈πn​(ℝ)G\in\pi_{n}(\mathbb{R}) have interspersed zeros but no common zeros, then we say that FF and GG have strictly interspersed zeros. All zeros of two polynomials with strictly interspersed zeros are simple and we will also say that polynomial F∈ℝ⁡[z]F\in\mathbb{R}[z] with only real simple zeros and the polynomial 00 have strictly interspersed zeros.

In [9, Lem. 1.55, 1.57] it is shown that polynomials with interspersed zeros can be characterized in the following way.

Lemma 11.

Let F∈πn​(ℝ)∖{0}F\in\pi_{n}(\mathbb{R})\setminus\{0\} and G∈ℝn​[z]∖{0}G\in\mathbb{R}_{n}[z]\setminus\{0\}.

  1. (a)

    FF and GG have strictly interspersed zeros if, and only if,

    F′​(z)​G​(z)−F⁡(z)​G′​(z)≠0for allz∈ℝ.F^{\prime}(z)G(z)-F(z)G^{\prime}(z)\neq 0\quad\mbox{for all}\quad z\in\mathbb{R}.
  2. (b)

    If F′​(z)​G​(z)−F⁡(z)​G′​(z)F^{\prime}(z)G(z)-F(z)G^{\prime}(z) is either non-positive or non-negative for all z∈ℝz\in\mathbb{R}, then FF and GG have interspersed zeros and F′​(z)​G​(z)−F⁡(z)​G′​(z)=0F^{\prime}(z)G(z)-F(z)G^{\prime}(z)=0 holds only if zz is a common zero of FF and GG.

  3. (c)

    If FF and GG have interspersed zeros, then (F/G)′​(z)(F/G)^{\prime}(z) is positive for every z∈ℝ¯z\in\overline{\mathbb{R}} or negative for every such zz.

For FF, G∈πn​(ℝ)G\in\pi_{n}(\mathbb{R}) we write F⪯GF\preceq G if F′​G−F​G′≤0F^{\prime}G-FG^{\prime}\leq 0 on ℝ\mathbb{R} (in particular F⪯0F\preceq 0 and 0⪯F0\preceq F for all F∈πn​(ℝ)F\in\pi_{n}(\mathbb{R})), and F≺GF\prec G if F⪯GF\preceq G and FF and GG have no common zeros. If F∈σn​(ℝ)F\in\sigma_{n}(\mathbb{R}) we also write 0≺F0\prec F and F≺0F\prec 0. By the above lemma, F⪯GF\preceq G implies that FF and GG have interspersed zeros; moreover, for FF,G​\nequiv​0G\nequiv 0 we have F≺GF\prec G if, and only if, F′​G−F​G′<0F^{\prime}G-FG^{\prime}<0 on ℝ\mathbb{R}.

Lemma 12.

Suppose FF, G∈ℝ⁡[z]∖{0}G\in\mathbb{R}[z]\setminus\{0\} satisfy F⪯GF\preceq G and F≠ℝGF\neq_{\mathbb{R}}G. Then for all s∈ℝs\in\mathbb{R} we have F+s​G⪯GF+sG\preceq G and F⪯G+s​FF\preceq G+sF. Furthermore, for s,t∈ℝs,t\in\mathbb{R} we have F+s​G⪯F+t​GF+sG\preceq F+tG and F+sG≠ℝF+tGF+sG\neq_{\mathbb{R}}F+tG if, and only if, s<ts<t.

(F+s​GF+t​G)′=(t−s)​F′​G−F​G′(F+t​G)2,(F+s​GG)′=(FG)′,(G+s​FF)′=(GF)′,\left(\frac{F+sG}{F+tG}\right)^{\prime}=\left(t-s\right)\frac{F^{\prime}G-FG^{\prime}}{\left(F+tG\right)^{2}},\quad\left(\frac{F+sG}{G}\right)^{\prime}=\left(\frac{F}{G}\right)^{\prime},\quad\left(\frac{G+sF}{F}\right)^{\prime}=\left(\frac{G}{F}\right)^{\prime},

and Lemma 11. ∎

The following characterization of interspersion is the essential ingredient of our proofs of Theorems 4 and 8. It is more or less equal to [10, Lemma 7], but, as explained in [34], it seems to have been known for a long time. To some extent, it can also be found in [17], for example. For the sake of completeness, we present a proof of it here.

for every zero yky_{k} of FF with G⁡(yk)≠0G(y_{k})\neq 0. This proves (a).

If F⪯GF\preceq G, then by Lemma 11(c) and the definition of ⪯\preceq we have (F/G)′​(z)<0(F/G)^{\prime}(z)<0 for all z∈ℝ¯z\in\overline{\mathbb{R}}. This implies cy<0c_{y}<0 for every n+1n+1-zero of FF that is not an n+1n+1-zero of GG by (10).

5. Polynomials with Log-Interspersed Zeros

It is obvious that for q∈(0,1)q\in(0,1) a polynomial F∈πn​(ℝ0−)F\in\pi_{n}(\mathbb{R}_{0}^{-}) belongs to 𝒩¯n​(q)\overline{\mathcal{N}}_{n}(q) if, and only if, F⁡(z)F(z) and F⁡(q−1​z)F(q^{-1}z) have interspersed zeros. It is also clear, however, that for no F∈ℛ¯n​(q)F\in\overline{\mathcal{R}}_{n}(q) that has both positive and negative zeros the polynomials F⁡(z)F(z) and F⁡(q−1​z)F(q^{-1}z) have interspersed zeros. We therefore need to extend the notion of interspersion in order to characterize all polynomials F∈ℛn​(q)F\in\mathcal{R}_{n}(q) in terms of the zero locations of F⁡(z)F(z) and F⁡(q−1​z)F(q^{-1}z).

For FF, G∈πn​(ℝ)G\in\pi_{n}(\mathbb{R}) we write F​\veebar​GF\veebar G if G⪯z​FG\preceq zF (in particular 0​\veebar​F0\veebar F and F​\veebar​0F\veebar 0 for all F∈πn​(ℝ)F\in\pi_{n}(\mathbb{R})). Moreover, we write F∨GF\vee G if F​\veebar​GF\veebar G and FF and GG have no common zeros expect possibly a common zero at the origin. Hence, if F≺0GF\prec_{0}G is supposed to mean that F⪯GF\preceq G and that FF and GG have no common zeros except possibly a common zero at the origin, then we have F∨GF\vee G if, and only if, G≺0zFG\prec_{0}zF. We shall also use the conventions 0∨F0\vee F, F∨0F\vee 0, 0≺0F0\prec_{0}F, and F≺00F\prec_{0}0, for all polynomials F∈πn​(ℝ)F\in\pi_{n}(\mathbb{R}) which have a multiple zero at most at the origin.

It is easy to see that F​\veebar​GF\veebar G implies deg⁡F≤deg⁡G≤2+deg⁡F\deg F\leq\deg G\leq 2+\deg F. We say that GG log-intersperses FF if F​\veebar​GF\veebar G or F​\veebar−GF\veebar-G. GG strictly log-intersperses FF if GG log-intersperses FF but FF and GG have no common zeros except possibly a common zero at the origin.

The next lemma gives a characterization of the relation F​\veebar​GF\veebar G in terms of the zeros of FF and GG.

This implies limz→y1−z​F​(z)/G⁡(z)=+∞\lim_{z\rightarrow y_{1}^{-}}zF(z)/G(z)=+\infty in the case y1<0y_{1}<0. belongs to 𝒩n​(q)\mathcal{N}_{n}(q), is of degree nn, and does not vanish at the origin. (1) and (28) show that

as ν→∞\nu\rightarrow\infty, and thus it follows that Fν→FF_{\nu}\rightarrow F locally uniformly on ℂ\mathbb{C} as ν→∞\nu\rightarrow\infty.

In the same way one constructs polynomials G^ν∈σn​(ℝ0−)\hat{G}_{\nu}\in\sigma_{n}(\mathbb{R}_{0}^{-}) with G^ν​(0)≠0\hat{G}_{\nu}(0)\neq 0 and deg⁡G^ν=n\deg\hat{G}_{\nu}=n that approximate GG. For q∈(0,1)q\in(0,1) the qq-difference operator Δq,n\Delta_{q,n} is defined by

Δq,n​[F]​(z):=F⁡(z)−F⁡(q−1​z)qn−1​z−q−1​z,F∈ℝn​[z].\Delta_{q,n}[F](z):=\frac{F(z)-F(q^{-1}z)}{q^{n-1}z-q^{-1}z},\quad F\in\mathbb{R}_{n}[z].

Using (2), it is easy to check that if FF is of the form F⁡(z)=∑k=0nCkn​(q)​ak​zkF(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}C_{k}^{n}(q)a_{k}z^{k}, then

(29) Δq,n​[F]​(z)=∑k=0n−1Ckn−1​(q)​ak+1​zkandΔq,n∗​[F]​(z)=∑k=0n−1Ckn−1​(q)​ak​zk.\Delta_{q,n}[F](z)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}C_{k}^{n-1}(q)a_{k+1}z^{k}\quad\mbox{and}\quad\Delta_{q,n}^{*}[F](z)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}C_{k}^{n-1}(q)a_{k}z^{k}.

limq→1Δq,n​[F]​(z)=limq→1∑k=0n−1Ckn−1​(q)​(nk+1)​ak+1Ck+1n​(q)​zk=∑k=0n−1(n−1k)​ak+1​zk=F′​(z)n,\lim_{q\rightarrow 1}\Delta_{q,n}[F](z)=\lim_{q\rightarrow 1}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}C_{k}^{n-1}(q)\frac{{n\choose k+1}a_{k+1}}{C_{k+1}^{n}(q)}z^{k}=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}{n-1\choose k}a_{k+1}z^{k}=\frac{F^{\prime}(z)}{n},

limq→1Δq,n∗​[F]​(z)=F⁡(z)−z​F′​(z)n.\lim_{q\rightarrow 1}\Delta_{q,n}^{*}[F](z)=F(z)-z\frac{F^{\prime}(z)}{n}.

We therefore set

(30) Δ1,n​[F]​(z):=F′​(z)nandΔ1,n∗​[F]​(z):=F⁡(z)−z​F′​(z)n,F∈ℝn​[z].\Delta_{1,n}[F](z):=\frac{F^{\prime}(z)}{n}\quad\mbox{and}\quad\Delta_{1,n}^{*}[F](z):=F(z)-z\frac{F^{\prime}(z)}{n},\quad F\in\mathbb{R}_{n}[z].

These observations show that Δq,n​[F]\Delta_{q,n}[F] is a qq-extension of the derivative F′F^{\prime}, while Δq,n∗​[F]\Delta_{q,n}^{*}[F] is a qq-extension of the polar derivative of FF with respect to 00 (cf. [20, (3.1.4)]). The next theorem is therefore a qq-extension of Rolle’s theorem.

Theorem 25 (qq-extension of Rolle’s theorem).

Let q∈(0,1]q\in(0,1].

  1. (a)

    If F∈ℛ¯n​(q)F\in\overline{\mathcal{R}}_{n}(q), then Δq,n​[F]∈ℛ¯n−1​(q)\Delta_{q,n}[F]\in\overline{\mathcal{R}}_{n-1}(q) and Δq,n​[F]⪯F\Delta_{q,n}[F]\preceq F. If F∈ℛn​(q)F\in\mathcal{R}_{n}(q), then Δq,n​[F]∈ℛn−1​(q)\Delta_{q,n}[F]\in\mathcal{R}_{n-1}(q) and Δq,n[F]≺0F\Delta_{q,n}[F]\prec_{0}F.

    If F∈𝒩¯n​(q)F\in\overline{\mathcal{N}}_{n}(q), then Δq,n​[F]∈𝒩¯n−1​(q)\Delta_{q,n}[F]\in\overline{\mathcal{N}}_{n-1}(q) and Δq,n​[F]⊴F\Delta_{q,n}[F]\unlhd F. If F∈𝒩n​(q)F\in\mathcal{N}_{n}(q), then Δq,n​[F]∈𝒩n−1​(q)\Delta_{q,n}[F]\in\mathcal{N}_{n-1}(q) and Δq,n​[F]⊲F\Delta_{q,n}[F]\lhd F.

Proof.

We will first verify (a). For n=0,1n=0,1 the assertions in (a) are trivial and therefore we assume that n≥2n\geq 2.

The case q=1q=1 is the classical theorem of Rolle together with the observation that n​F​(z)/(z​F′​(z))→1nF(z)/(zF^{\prime}(z))\rightarrow 1 as z→∞z\rightarrow\infty and that therefore n​F​(z)/F′​(z)nF(z)/F^{\prime}(z) has to be increasing for large z>0z>0.

In order to prove the case q∈(0,1)q\in(0,1), suppose first that FF lies in ℛn​(q)\mathcal{R}_{n}(q), is of degree nn, and satisfies F⁡(0)≠0F(0)\neq 0. Then there is a k∈{0,…,n}k\in\{0,\ldots,n\} such that FF has nn distinct zeros xjx_{j} which satisfy

Because of Rolle’s theorem for every j∈{1,…,n−1}j\in\{1,\ldots,n-1\} there is exactly one critical point yjy_{j} of FF in (xj,xj+1)(x_{j},x_{j+1}). We will now prove the assertion in the case where T:=F⁡(yk)>0T:=F(y_{k})>0 and yk>0y_{k}>0 (the other possible cases can be verified in a similar manner).

Under this assumption there are continuous functions a⁡(t)∈[xk,yk]a(t)\in[x_{k},y_{k}] and b⁡(t)∈[yk,xk+1]b(t)\in[y_{k},x_{k+1}] with

Consequently, a⁡(0)=xka(0)=x_{k}, b⁡(0)=xk+1b(0)=x_{k+1}, and a⁡(T)=b⁡(T)=yka(T)=b(T)=y_{k}. Since r⁡(t):=a⁡(t)/b⁡(t)r(t):=a(t)/b(t) is continuous in [0,T][0,T] with r⁡(0)=xk/xk+1≤0r(0)=x_{k}/x_{k+1}\leq 0 and r⁡(T)=1r(T)=1 there must be a t0∈(0,T)t_{0}\in(0,T) (actually, t0∈(F⁡(0),T)t_{0}\in(F(0),T)) with r⁡(t0)=qr(t_{0})=q. Setting wk:=a⁡(t0)w_{k}:=a(t_{0}), this means b⁡(t0)=q−1​wkb(t_{0})=q^{-1}w_{k} and thus, because of (31), Δq,n​[F]​(wk)=0\Delta_{q,n}[F](w_{k})=0. Moreover,

(32) xk<0<wk<q−1​wk<xk+1.x_{k}<0<w_{k}<q^{-1}w_{k}<x_{k+1}.

Since F∈ℛn​(q)F\in\mathcal{R}_{n}(q) we have xj/xj+1<qx_{j}/x_{j+1}<q for j∈{k+1,…,n−1}j\in\{k+1,\ldots,n-1\} and j∈{1,…,k−1}j\in\{1,\ldots,k-1\}. Making use of these inequalities, we can proceed in a similar way as in the case j=kj=k to find that Δq,n​[F]\Delta_{q,n}[F] has zeros wjw_{j}, j∈{1,…,n−1}∖{k}j\in\{1,\ldots,n-1\}\setminus\{k\}, with

xj<q−1​wj<wj<xj+1,\displaystyle x_{j}<q^{-1}w_{j}<w_{j}<x_{j+1}, for ​j∈{1,…,k−1},\displaystyle\quad\mbox{for }j\in\{1,\ldots,k-1\},
xj<wj<q−1​wj<xj+1,\displaystyle x_{j}<w_{j}<q^{-1}w_{j}<x_{j+1}, for j∈{k+1,…,n−1}.\displaystyle\quad\mbox{for }j\in\{k+1,\ldots,n-1\}.

This, together with (32), shows that Δq,n​[F]∈ℛn−1​(q)\Delta_{q,n}[F]\in\mathcal{R}_{n-1}(q) and that FF and Δq,n​[F]\Delta_{q,n}[F] have strictly interspersed zeros. By (2) we have

F⁡(z)z​Δq,n​[F]​(z)→Ckn​(q)Ck−1n−1​(q)>0asz→∞.\frac{F(z)}{z\Delta_{q,n}[F](z)}\rightarrow\frac{C_{k}^{n}(q)}{C_{k-1}^{n-1}(q)}>0\quad\mbox{as}\quad z\rightarrow\infty.

Hence, F⁡(z)/Δq,n​[F]​(z)F(z)/\Delta_{q,n}[F](z) is increasing for large zz, which implies Δq,n​[F]≺F\Delta_{q,n}[F]\prec F since FF and Δq,n​[F]\Delta_{q,n}[F] have strictly interspersed zeros.

It remains to prove (a) for F∈ℛ¯n​(q)F\in\overline{\mathcal{R}}_{n}(q) or F∈ℛn​(q)F\in\mathcal{R}_{n}(q) which do not have to be of degree nn and ≠0\neq 0 at z=0z=0. If FF is a polynomial in ℛ¯n​(q)\overline{\mathcal{R}}_{n}(q), then Lemma 24 and what we have just shown yield Δq,n​[F]∈ℛ¯n−1​(q)\Delta_{q,n}[F]\in\overline{\mathcal{R}}_{n-1}(q) and Δq,n​[F]⪯F\Delta_{q,n}[F]\preceq F. If Δq,n​[F]\Delta_{q,n}[F] and FF have a common zero at a point z∈ℝ∖{0}z\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}, then it follows that F⁡(z)=F⁡(q−1​z)=0F(z)=F(q^{-1}z)=0 and hence that F∉ℛn​(q)F\notin\mathcal{R}_{n}(q). If there is a z>0z>0 (in the case z<0z<0 one can argue analogously) such that Δq,n​[F]​(z)=Δq,n​[F]​(q−1​z)=0\Delta_{q,n}[F](z)=\Delta_{q,n}[F](q^{-1}z)=0, then

Hence, FF and F′F^{\prime} would not have interspersed zeros, a contradiction to the fact that FF has only real zeros. We can suppose that x∈[z,q−1​z]x\in[z,q^{-1}z]. Then because of (33) there has to a second zero yy of FF in [z,q−1​z][z,q^{-1}z]. The proof of (a) also shows that if FF belongs to 𝒩¯n​(q)\overline{\mathcal{N}}_{n}(q) or 𝒩n​(q)\mathcal{N}_{n}(q), then Δq,n​[F]\Delta_{q,n}[F] belongs to, respectively, 𝒩¯n−1​(q)\overline{\mathcal{N}}_{n-1}(q) or 𝒩n−1​(q)\mathcal{N}_{n-1}(q). (b) thus follows from (a) and the definition of ⊴\unlhd. ∎

Theorem 26.

Let q∈(0,1]q\in(0,1] and suppose 𝒞\mathcal{C} denotes one of the classes ℛ¯n​(q)\overline{\mathcal{R}}_{n}(q), ℛn​(q)\mathcal{R}_{n}(q), 𝒩¯n​(q)\overline{\mathcal{N}}_{n}(q), 𝒩n​(q)\mathcal{N}_{n}(q). Then F∈𝒞F\in\mathcal{C} implies Δq,n∗​[F]∈𝒞\Delta_{q,n}^{*}[F]\in\mathcal{C}.

(Δq,n​[F])∗(n−1)​(z)=\displaystyle\left(\Delta_{q,n}[F]\right)^{*(n-1)}(z)=\; zn−1​F⁡(−z−1)−F⁡(−q−1​z−1)−qn−1​z−1+q−1​z−1\displaystyle z^{n-1}\frac{F(-z^{-1})-F(-q^{-1}z^{-1})}{-q^{n-1}z^{-1}+q^{-1}z^{-1}}
=\displaystyle=\; −q1−n​q−n​F∗n​(q​z)−F∗n​(z)q−n−1=−q1−n​Δq,n∗​[F∗n]​(q​z).\displaystyle-q^{1-n}\frac{q^{-n}F^{*n}(qz)-F^{*n}(z)}{q^{-n}-1}=-q^{1-n}\Delta_{q,n}^{*}[F^{*n}](qz).

z​(F∗n)′​(z)n−F∗n​(z)=(F′​(z)n)∗(n−1)z\frac{(F^{*n})^{\prime}(z)}{n}-F^{*n}(z)=\left(\frac{F^{\prime}(z)}{n}\right)^{*(n-1)}

and thus, for all q∈(0,1]q\in(0,1] and F∈ℝn​[z]F\in\mathbb{R}_{n}[z], we have

(34) (Δq,n​[F])∗(n−1)​(z)=−q1−n​Δq,n∗​[F∗n]​(q​z).\left(\Delta_{q,n}[F]\right)^{*(n-1)}(z)=-q^{1-n}\Delta_{q,n}^{*}[F^{*n}](qz).

Together with Theorem 25, this relation immediately shows that if FF belongs to ℛ¯n​(q)\overline{\mathcal{R}}_{n}(q) or ℛn​(q)\mathcal{R}_{n}(q), then Δq,n∗​[F]\Delta_{q,n}^{*}[F] is an element of, respectively, ℛ¯n−1​(q)\overline{\mathcal{R}}_{n-1}(q) or ℛn−1​(q)\mathcal{R}_{n-1}(q).

Δq,n​[F⁡(−z)]​(z)=−Δq,n​[F]​(−z),\Delta_{q,n}[F(-z)](z)=-\Delta_{q,n}[F](-z),

(34) and Theorem 25 therefore also give the remaining parts of the assertion. ∎

As described in Section 2.3 ”Newton’s inequalities” [31, Thm. 2] state that if F⁡(z)=∑k=0n(nk)​ak​zkF(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}{n\choose k}a_{k}z^{k} is an element of ℛ¯n​(1)\overline{\mathcal{R}}_{n}(1), then the sequence {ak}k=0n\{a_{k}\}_{k=0}^{n} is log-concave. Using Theorems 25 and 26 the proof of Newton’s inequalities (as given in [31, Thm. 2], for example) can be modified in order to obtain the following.

Theorem 27.

(qq-extension of Newton’s inequalities) Let q∈(0,1]q\in(0,1] and suppose F⁡(z)=∑k=0nCkn​(q)​ak​zk∈ℛn​(q)F(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}C_{k}^{n}(q)a_{k}z^{k}\in\mathcal{R}_{n}(q). Then f⁡(z):=∑k=0nak​zkf(z):=\sum_{k=0}^{n}a_{k}z^{k} belongs to ℒ​𝒞n\mathcal{LC}_{n}, i.e. we have

ak2>ak−1​ak+1for allk∈{0,…,n}a_{k}^{2}>a_{k-1}a_{k+1}\quad\mbox{for all}\quad k\in\{0,\ldots,n\}

for which there are l≤kl\leq k and m≥km\geq k such that ala_{l}, am≠0a_{m}\neq 0. If F∈𝒩n​(q)F\in\mathcal{N}_{n}(q), then ff belongs to ℒ​𝒞n+\mathcal{LC}_{n}^{+}, i.e. f∈ℒ​𝒞nf\in\mathcal{LC}_{n} and all coefficients are either non-positive or non-negative.

Proof.

Applying Theorem 25 j−1j-1-times to F⁡(z)=∑k=0nCkn​(q)​ak​zk∈ℛn​(q)F(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}C_{k}^{n}(q)a_{k}z^{k}\in\mathcal{R}_{n}(q) yields that

∑k=0n−j+1Ckn−j+1​(q)​ak+j−1​zk∈ℛn−j+1​(q),\sum_{k=0}^{n-j+1}C_{k}^{n-j+1}(q)a_{k+j-1}z^{k}\in\mathcal{R}_{n-j+1}(q),

and applying Theorem 26 n−j−1n-j-1-times to this polynomial leads to

p⁡(z):=q​aj+1​z2+(1+q)​aj​z+aj−1=∑k=02Ck2​(q)​ak+j−1​zk∈ℛ2​(q).p(z):=qa_{j+1}z^{2}+(1+q)a_{j}z+a_{j-1}=\sum_{k=0}^{2}C_{k}^{2}(q)a_{k+j-1}z^{k}\in\mathcal{R}_{2}(q).

By [14, VIII. Lem. 3] we have aj+1​aj−1<0≤aj2a_{j+1}a_{j-1}<0\leq a_{j}^{2} for every j∈{ord⁡(F;0)+1,…,−1+deg⁡F}j\in\{\operatorname{ord}(F;0)+1,\ldots,-1+\deg F\} with aj=0a_{j}=0. We can therefore assume that aj+1​aj−1≠0a_{j+1}a_{j-1}\neq 0. Then

z1,2:=−(1+q)​aj±(1+q)2​aj2−4​q​aj+1​aj−12​q​aj+1z_{1,2}:=\frac{-(1+q)a_{j}\pm\sqrt{(1+q)^{2}a_{j}^{2}-4qa_{j+1}a_{j-1}}}{2qa_{j+1}}

are the zeros of pp. It follows that

z1​z2=aj−1q​aj+1z_{1}z_{2}=\frac{a_{j-1}}{qa_{j+1}}

and hence that aj+1​aj−1<0≤aj2a_{j+1}a_{j-1}<0\leq a_{j}^{2} if z1​z2<0z_{1}z_{2}<0.

If z1​z2>0z_{1}z_{2}>0, then we can assume that z1,z2<0z_{1},z_{2}<0 (by considering p⁡(−z)p(-z) instead of p⁡(z)p(z) if necessary). Then aj+1,aj,aj−1a_{j+1},a_{j},a_{j-1} must be all of same sign and we can assume that they are all positive. Since p∈ℛ2​(q)p\in\mathcal{R}_{2}(q), we have q​z2<z1<0qz_{2}<z_{1}<0, and hence that

q>4​q​aj+1​aj−1((1+q)​aj+(1+q)2​aj2−4​q​aj+1​aj−1)2=q(x+x2−q)2,q>\frac{4qa_{j+1}a_{j-1}}{\left((1+q)a_{j}+\sqrt{(1+q)^{2}a_{j}^{2}-4qa_{j+1}a_{j-1}}\right)^{2}}=\frac{q}{\left(x+\sqrt{x^{2}-q}\right)^{2}},

with x:=(1+q)​aj/4​aj+1​aj−1x:=(1+q)a_{j}/\sqrt{4a_{j+1}a_{j-1}}. This inequality implies x2−q>1−x\sqrt{x^{2}-q}>1-x and thus

(1+q)​aj2​aj+1​aj−1=x>1+q2.\frac{(1+q)a_{j}}{2\sqrt{a_{j+1}a_{j-1}}}=x>\frac{1+q}{2}.

This is equivalent to aj2>aj+1​aj−1a_{j}^{2}>a_{j+1}a_{j-1} and therefore proves the assertion for F∈ℛn​(q)F\in\mathcal{R}_{n}(q). Since all coefficients of a polynomial with only non-positive zeros are of same sign, this also verifies the assertion for F∈𝒩n​(q)F\in\mathcal{N}_{n}(q). ∎

It follows from (30) that

Δ1,n∗​[F]+x​Δ1,n​[F]\Delta_{1,n}^{*}[F]+x\Delta_{1,n}[F]

is equal (up to a factor nn) to the polar derivative of a polynomial F∈ℝn​[z]F\in\mathbb{R}_{n}[z] with respect to xx. Laguerre’s theorem states that all zeros of this polar derivative are real if F∈πn​(ℝ)F\in\pi_{n}(\mathbb{R}) and x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R} (cf. [20, Thm. 3.2.1]). Because of [16, Satz 5.2] this means that Δ1,n​[F]\Delta_{1,n}[F] and Δ1,n∗​[F]\Delta_{1,n}^{*}[F] have interspersed zeros. The next theorem is therefore a qq-extension of Laguerre’s theorem.

Theorem 28 (qq-extension of Laguerre’s theorem).

Let q∈(0,1]q\in(0,1].

  1. (a)

    If F∈ℛ¯n​(q)F\in\overline{\mathcal{R}}_{n}(q), then Δq,n​[F]⪯Δq,n∗​[F]\Delta_{q,n}[F]\preceq\Delta_{q,n}^{*}[F]. If F∈ℛn​(q)F\in\mathcal{R}_{n}(q), then Δq,n[F]≺0Δq,n∗[F]\Delta_{q,n}[F]\prec_{0}\Delta_{q,n}^{*}[F].

  2. (b)

    If F∈𝒩¯n​(q)F\in\overline{\mathcal{N}}_{n}(q), then Δq,n​[F]⊴Δq,n∗​[F]\Delta_{q,n}[F]\unlhd\Delta_{q,n}^{*}[F]. If F∈𝒩n​(q)F\in\mathcal{N}_{n}(q), then Δq,n​[F]⊲Δq,n∗​[F]\Delta_{q,n}[F]\lhd\Delta_{q,n}^{*}[F].

Proof.

By Theorems 25 and 26 we have Δq,n​[F]\Delta_{q,n}[F], Δq,n∗​[F]∈πn​(ℝ0−)\Delta_{q,n}^{*}[F]\in\pi_{n}(\mathbb{R}_{0}^{-}) when F∈𝒩¯n​(q)F\in\overline{\mathcal{N}}_{n}(q). Since all coefficients of a polynomial in πn​(ℝ0−)\pi_{n}(\mathbb{R}_{0}^{-}) must be of same sign, we also have (Δq,n​[F]/Δq,n∗​[F])​(z)>0(\Delta_{q,n}[F]/\Delta_{q,n}^{*}[F])(z)>0 for all z>0z>0 when F∈𝒩¯n​(q)F\in\overline{\mathcal{N}}_{n}(q). (b) therefore follows directly from (a) and Lemma 18.

In order to prove (a), we can assume that n≥2n\geq 2. We will first suppose that q∈(0,1)q\in(0,1) and that FF is an element of ℛn​(q)\mathcal{R}_{n}(q) which is of degree nn and does not vanish at the origin.

Proof of Theorem 4.

For 0<r<q≤10<r<q\leq 1 Statements (a)–(c) follow readily from Theorem 31. Moreover, (a) and (b) are trivial for q=0q=0. If we denote the open upper half-plane by 𝕌\mathbb{U}, then the Hermite-Biehler theorem [20, Thm. 6.3.4] states that

Theorem 33.

8. An extension of Ruscheweyh’s convolution lemma

In this section we will prove the extension of Ruscheweyh’s convolution lemma that is given by Lemma 8. We will obtain Lemma 8 as a limit case of a version of Lemma 16 in which polynomials which are symmetric with respect to ℝ\mathbb{R} (i.e. real polynomials) are replaced by polynomials which are symmetric with respect to 𝕋\mathbb{T} (so-called self-inversive polynomials). Lemma 16 can therefore be seen as the real polynomial version of Ruscheweyh’s convolution lemma. The necessary definitions regarding self-inversive polynomials are as follows.

The nn-inverse of a polynomial F⁡(z)=∑k=0nak​zkF(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}a_{k}z^{k} of degree ≤n\leq n is defined by

In​[F]​(z):=zn​F⁡(1z¯)¯=∑k=0na¯n−k​zkI_{n}[F](z):=z^{n}\overline{F\left(\frac{1}{\overline{z}}\right)}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\overline{a}_{n-k}z^{k}

and FF is called nn-self-inversive if F=In​[F]F=I_{n}[F] (in particular 00 is nn-self-inversive for all n∈ℕ0n\in\mathbb{N}_{0}). The zeros of In​[F]I_{n}[F] are obtained by reflecting the zeros of FF with respect to 𝕋\mathbb{T}. Hence, if F∈πn​(𝔻)F\in\pi_{n}(\mathbb{D}), then F/In​[F]F/I_{n}[F] is a Blaschke product, and therefore, for those FF, we have F+ζ​In​[F]∈πn​(𝕋)F+\zeta I_{n}[F]\in\pi_{n}(\mathbb{T}) for all ζ∈𝕋\zeta\in\mathbb{T}. The zero reflection property of In​[F]I_{n}[F] also shows that the zeros of nn-self-inversive polynomials lie symmetrically around 𝕋\mathbb{T}. Furthermore, it is easy to see that every polynomial of degree ≤n\leq n with zeros symmetrically around 𝕋\mathbb{T} is nn-self-inversive up to a constant multiple of modulus 11.

It is clear that F⁡(z)=∑k=0nak​zkF(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}a_{k}z^{k} is nn-self-inversive if, and only if, ak=a¯n−ka_{k}=\overline{a}_{n-k} for all k∈{0,…,n}k\in\{0,\ldots,n\} and therefore 𝒮​ℐn\mathcal{SI}_{n}, the set of all nn-self-inversive polynomials, is a real vector space of dimension n+1n+1. The coefficient symmetry of nn-self-inversive polynomials also implies that for F∈𝒮​ℐnF\in\mathcal{SI}_{n} we have e−int/2F(ei​t)∈ℝe^{-int/2}F(e^{it})\in\mathbb{R} for all t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}.

Lemma 34.
  2. (a)

    For all F∈ℂn​[z]F\in\mathbb{C}_{n}[z] and m∈ℕ0m\in\mathbb{N}_{0} we have F+zm​In​[F]∈𝒮​ℐn+mF+z^{m}I_{n}[F]\in\mathcal{SI}_{n+m}.

  3. (b)

    For all F∈πn​(ℂ∖𝔻)F\in\pi_{n}(\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{D}) and m∈ℕ0m\in\mathbb{N}_{0} we have F+zm​In​[F]∈πn+m​(𝕋)F+z^{m}I_{n}[F]\in\pi_{n+m}(\mathbb{T}).

Proof.

We have

In+m​[F+zm​In​[F]]=In+m​[F]+In+m​[zm​In​[F]]=zm​In​[F]+FI_{n+m}[F+z^{m}I_{n}[F]]=I_{n+m}[F]+I_{n+m}[z^{m}I_{n}[F]]=z^{m}I_{n}[F]+F

and thus (a) is clear. Since the zeros of In​[F]I_{n}[F] are obtained by reflecting the zeros of FF around 𝕋\mathbb{T}, In​[F]/FI_{n}[F]/F, and thus also zm​In​[F]/Fz^{m}I_{n}[F]/F, is a Blaschke product when F∈πn​(ℂ∖𝔻)F\in\pi_{n}(\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{D}). Since a Blaschke product can take the value 11 only on 𝕋\mathbb{T}, (a) is also proven. ∎

We say that FF, G∈πn​(𝕋)G\in\pi_{n}(\mathbb{T}) have 𝕋\mathbb{T}-interspersed zeros if the zeros of FF and GG alternate on the unit circle. If FF and GG have 𝕋\mathbb{T}-interspersed zeros, but no common zeros, then FF and GG are said to have strictly 𝕋\mathbb{T}-interspersed zeros. The following analogue of Lemma 11 holds for 𝕋\mathbb{T}-interspersion: F∈πn​(𝕋)F\in\pi_{n}(\mathbb{T}) and G∈𝒮​ℐn∖{0}G\in\mathcal{SI}_{n}\setminus\{0\} have 𝕋\mathbb{T}-interspersed zeros if, and only if, the real valued function

t↦F⁡(ei​t)G⁡(ei​t)=e−int/2F(ei​t)e−int/2G(ei​t),t∈ℝ,t\mapsto\frac{F(e^{it})}{G(e^{it})}=\frac{e^{-int/2}F(e^{it})}{e^{-int/2}G(e^{it})},\qquad t\in\mathbb{R},

is either strictly increasing on ℝ\mathbb{R} or strictly decreasing on ℝ\mathbb{R}. Similarly to the real case we therefore write F⪯𝕋GF\preceq_{\mathbb{T}}G if FF, G∈πn​(𝕋)G\in\pi_{n}(\mathbb{T}) satisfy

(e−int/2F(ei​t))′(e−int/2G(ei​t))−(e−int/2F(ei​t))(e−int/2G(ei​t))′≤0fort∈ℝ,(e^{-int/2}F(e^{it}))^{\prime}(e^{-int/2}G(e^{it}))-(e^{-int/2}F(e^{it}))(e^{-int/2}G(e^{it}))^{\prime}\leq 0\quad\mbox{for}\quad t\in\mathbb{R},

and F≺𝕋GF\prec_{\mathbb{T}}G if F⪯𝕋GF\preceq_{\mathbb{T}}G and FF and GG do not have common zeros. It is then easy to see that the following holds.

Lemma 35.

Let FF, G∈𝒮​ℐnG\in\mathcal{SI}_{n}. Then F⪯𝕋GF\preceq_{\mathbb{T}}G if, and only if, Im⁡(F/G)​(z)<0\operatorname{Im}\,(F/G)(z)<0 for z∈𝔻z\in\mathbb{D}.

Using the Möbius transformation i⁡(1+z)/(1−z)i(1+z)/(1-z) we can transfer Lemma 16 to nn-self-inversive polynomials as follows.

Lemma 36.

Let L:𝒮​ℐn→𝒮​ℐmL:\mathcal{SI}_{n}\rightarrow\mathcal{SI}_{m} be a real linear operator and suppose FF, G∈𝒮​ℐnG\in\mathcal{SI}_{n} are such that F/G=P/QF/G=P/Q with polynomials PP, QQ that have zeros only on 𝕋\mathbb{T} and satisfy P≺𝕋QP\prec_{\mathbb{T}}Q. Let 𝒵\mathcal{Z} denote the set of y∈{ei​t:0≤t<π}y\in\{e^{it}:0\leq t<\pi\} for which −y2-y^{2} is a zero of F/GF/G. If for every y∈𝒵y\in\mathcal{Z}

(45) L[(1+z)​Fy+y¯​z]⪯𝕋L[i⁡(1−z)​Fy+y¯​z]L\left[\frac{(1+z)F}{y+\overline{y}z}\right]\preceq_{\mathbb{T}}L\left[\frac{i(1-z)F}{y+\overline{y}z}\right]

then L[F]⪯𝕋L[G]L[F]\preceq_{\mathbb{T}}L[G]. If (45) holds with ⪯𝕋\preceq_{\mathbb{T}} replaced by ≺𝕋\prec_{\mathbb{T}} for one y∈𝒵y\in\mathcal{Z}, then L[F]≺𝕋L[G]L[F]\prec_{\mathbb{T}}L[G].

Proof.

Set

ψ⁡(z):=i​1+z1−zand note thatψ(−1)​(z)=z−iz+i.\psi(z):=i\frac{1+z}{1-z}\quad\mbox{and note that}\quad\psi^{(-1)}(z)=\frac{z-i}{z+i}.

Then

Ψn​[H]​(z):=(z+i)n​H​(ψ(−1)​(z)),H∈ℂn​[z],\Psi_{n}[H](z):=(z+i)^{n}H(\psi^{(-1)}(z)),\qquad H\in\mathbb{C}_{n}[z],

with inverse

Ψn(−1)​[H]​(z):=1(2​i)n​(1−z)n​H​(ψ⁡(z))\Psi_{n}^{(-1)}[H](z):=\frac{1}{(2i)^{n}}(1-z)^{n}H(\psi(z))

is an isomorphism between 𝒮​ℐn\mathcal{SI}_{n} and ℝn​[z]\mathbb{R}_{n}[z] which maps πn​(𝕋)\pi_{n}(\mathbb{T}) onto πn​(ℝ)\pi_{n}(\mathbb{R}) and σn​(𝕋)\sigma_{n}(\mathbb{T}) onto σn​(ℝ)\sigma_{n}(\mathbb{R}). Moreover, since (ψ⁡(ei​t))′>0(\psi(e^{it}))^{\prime}>0 for t∈(0,2​π)t\in(0,2\pi), Ψn\Psi_{n} preserves position, i.e. we have F⪯𝕋GF\preceq_{\mathbb{T}}G and F≺𝕋GF\prec_{\mathbb{T}}G if, and only if, Ψn​[F]⪯Ψn​[G]\Psi_{n}[F]\preceq\Psi_{n}[G] and Ψn​[F]≺Ψn​[G]\Psi_{n}[F]\prec\Psi_{n}[G], respectively.

Straightforward calculations show that if y∈𝒵y\in\mathcal{Z}, then

(46) Ψn​[(1+z)​Fy+y¯​z]=2y+y¯​z​Ψn​[F]z−ψ⁡(−y2)andΨn​[i⁡(1−z)​Fy+y¯​z]=−2y+y¯​Ψn​[F]z−ψ⁡(−y2)\Psi_{n}\left[\frac{(1+z)F}{y+\overline{y}z}\right]=\frac{2}{y+\overline{y}}\frac{z\Psi_{n}[F]}{z-\psi(-y^{2})}\quad\mbox{and}\quad\Psi_{n}\left[\frac{i(1-z)F}{y+\overline{y}z}\right]=\frac{-2}{y+\overline{y}}\frac{\Psi_{n}[F]}{z-\psi(-y^{2})}

if y≠iy\neq i, and

(47) Ψn​[(1+z)​Fy+y¯​z]=−z​Ψn​[F]andΨn​[i⁡(1−z)​Fy+y¯​z]=Ψn​[F]\Psi_{n}\left[\frac{(1+z)F}{y+\overline{y}z}\right]=-z\Psi_{n}[F]\quad\mbox{and}\quad\Psi_{n}\left[\frac{i(1-z)F}{y+\overline{y}z}\right]=\Psi_{n}[F]

if y=iy=i. Note that Ψn​[F]\Psi_{n}[F] is of degree nn if, and only if, i∉𝒵i\notin\mathcal{Z} and that {ψ⁡(−y2):y∈𝒵∖{0}}\{\psi(-y^{2}):y\in\mathcal{Z}\setminus\{0\}\} is the set of zeros of Ψn​[F]\Psi_{n}[F].

Hence, if we set A:=Ψn​[F]A:=\Psi_{n}[F] and define

K:ℝn​[z]→ℝm​[z],H↦(Ψm∘L∘Ψn(−1))​[H],K:\mathbb{R}_{n}[z]\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{m}[z],\,H\mapsto(\Psi_{m}\circ L\circ\Psi_{n}^{(-1)})[H],

then it follows from (45), (47), and the fact that Ψn\Psi_{n} preserves position, that

(48) K⁡[A∞]⪯K⁡[A]ifdeg⁡A<n,K[A_{\infty}]\preceq K[A]\quad\mbox{if}\quad\deg A<n,

and from (45) and (46) that K⁡[z​Ax]⪯−K⁡[Ax]K[zA_{x}]\preceq-K[A_{x}] for every zero xx of AA. Because of Lemma 12 this implies K⁡[A]=K⁡[z​Ax]−x​K​[Ax]⪯−K⁡[Ax]K[A]=K[zA_{x}]-xK[A_{x}]\preceq-K[A_{x}], and thus we obtain

(49) K⁡[Ax]⪯K⁡[A]for every zeroxofA.K[A_{x}]\preceq K[A]\quad\mbox{for every zero}\quad x\quad\mbox{of}\quad A.

Since Ψn\Psi_{n} preserves position, F⪯𝕋GF\preceq_{\mathbb{T}}G implies A⪯BA\preceq B, with B:=Ψn​[G]B:=\Psi_{n}[G]. It therefore follows from (48), (49), and Lemma 16, that K⁡[A]⪯K⁡[B]K[A]\preceq K[B]. This implies L[F]⪯𝕋L[G]L[F]\preceq_{\mathbb{T}}L[G] and the proof is complete. ∎

Lemma 37.

Let FF and GG be polynomials of degree ≤n\leq n that are such that

Im⁡F⁡(z)G⁡(z)<0forz∈𝔻.\operatorname{Im}\,\frac{F(z)}{G(z)}<0\quad\mbox{for}\quad z\in\mathbb{D}.

Then

Im⁡F⁡(z)+zn+1​In​[F]​(z)G⁡(z)+zn+1​In​[G]​(z)<0forz∈𝔻.\operatorname{Im}\,\frac{F(z)+z^{n+1}I_{n}[F](z)}{G(z)+z^{n+1}I_{n}[G](z)}<0\quad\mbox{for}\quad z\in\mathbb{D}.
Proof.

It follows from the assumptions that (F−x​G)​(z)≠0(F-xG)(z)\neq 0 for all x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R} and z∈𝔻z\in\mathbb{D}. By Lemma 34(b) this implies

F⁡(z)−x​G​(z)+zn+1​In​[F−x​G]​(z)≠0,F(z)-xG(z)+z^{n+1}I_{n}[F-xG](z)\neq 0,

or, equivalently, since InI_{n} is real linear,

F⁡(z)+zn+1​In​[F]​(z)G⁡(z)+zn+1​In​[G]​(z)≠x\frac{F(z)+z^{n+1}I_{n}[F](z)}{G(z)+z^{n+1}I_{n}[G](z)}\neq x

for all x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R} and z∈𝔻z\in\mathbb{D}. The assertion thus follows from the fact that Im⁡(F/G)​(0)<0\operatorname{Im}\,(F/G)(0)<0. ∎

Lemma 38.

Let L:ℋ⁡(𝔻)→ℋ⁡(𝔻)L:\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D})\rightarrow\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D}) be a continuous real linear operator. Suppose f∈ℋ⁡(𝔻)f\in\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D}) is such that

(50) ImL⁡[(1+z)​fy+y¯​z]L⁡[i⁡(1−z)​fy+y¯​z](z)<0for allz∈𝔻 and y∈𝕋 with Imy≥0.\operatorname{Im}\,\frac{L\left[\frac{(1+z)f}{y+\overline{y}z}\right]}{L\left[\frac{i(1-z)f}{y+\overline{y}z}\right]}(z)<0\quad\mbox{for all}\quad z\in\mathbb{D}\mbox{ and }y\in\mathbb{T}\mbox{ with }\operatorname{Im}\,y\geq 0.

Then for every g∈ℋ⁡(𝔻)g\in\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D}) which satisfies Im⁡(f/g)​(z)<0\operatorname{Im}\,(f/g)(z)<0 for z∈𝔻z\in\mathbb{D} we have

ImL⁡[f]L⁡[g](z)<0for z∈𝔻.\operatorname{Im}\,\frac{L\left[f\right]}{L\left[g\right]}(z)<0\quad\mbox{for }\quad z\in\mathbb{D}.

By considering h↦L​[h]​(r​z)h\mapsto L[h](rz), r∈(0,1)r\in(0,1), instead of LL, and f⁡(sr​z)f(s_{r}z) and g⁡(sr​z)g(s_{r}z) instead of ff and gg for a suitable function sr∈(0,1)s_{r}\in(0,1) with limr→1sr=1\lim_{r\rightarrow 1}s_{r}=1, we can assume that Im⁡(f/g)​(z)<0\operatorname{Im}\,(f/g)(z)<0 for z∈𝔻¯z\in\overline{\mathbb{D}} and that (50) holds for z∈𝔻¯z\in\overline{\mathbb{D}}.

Now, let

Φn:ℋ⁡(𝔻)→ℋ⁡(𝔻),∑k=0∞ak​zk↦∑k=0nak​zk\Phi_{n}:\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D})\rightarrow\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D}),\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_{k}z^{k}\mapsto\sum_{k=0}^{n}a_{k}z^{k}

and set

Ln​[h]:=(Φn∘L∘Φn)​[h]forh∈ℋ⁡(𝔻),n∈ℕ.L_{n}[h]:=(\Phi_{n}\circ L\circ\Phi_{n})[h]\quad\mbox{for}\quad h\in\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D}),\,n\in\mathbb{N}.

Then {Ln}n\{L_{n}\}_{n} is a pointwise convergent sequence of continuous linear operators and thus an equicontinuous family.

Setting hn:=Φn​[h]h_{n}:=\Phi_{n}[h] for h∈ℋ⁡(𝔻)h\in\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D}), it therefore follows from (50) and a compactness argument that there is an n0∈ℕn_{0}\in\mathbb{N} such that

(51) Im⁡Ln​[(1+z)​fny+y¯​z]Ln​[i⁡(1−z)​fny+y¯​z]​(z)<0for allz∈𝔻¯,y∈𝕋′:={z∈𝕋:Im⁡y≥0},n≥n0.\operatorname{Im}\,\frac{L_{n}\left[\frac{(1+z)f_{n}}{y+\overline{y}z}\right]}{L_{n}\left[\frac{i(1-z)f_{n}}{y+\overline{y}z}\right]}(z)<0\quad\mbox{for all}\quad z\in\overline{\mathbb{D}},\,y\in\mathbb{T}^{\prime}:=\{z\in\mathbb{T}:\operatorname{Im}\,y\geq 0\},\,n\geq n_{0}.

for all z∈𝔻z\in\mathbb{D}, n≥n0n\geq n_{0}, y∈𝕋′y\in\mathbb{T}^{\prime}.

Kn​[h]:=Ln​[h]+zn+1​(Ln​[h])∗n.K_{n}[h]:=L_{n}[h]+z^{n+1}(L_{n}[h])^{*n}.

Im⁡fn​(z)+zn+1​fn∗n​(z)gn​(z)+zn+1​gn∗n​(z)<0\operatorname{Im}\,\frac{f_{n}(z)+z^{n+1}f_{n}^{*n}(z)}{g_{n}(z)+z^{n+1}g_{n}^{*n}(z)}<0

Proof of Lemma 8.

Writing x=(1+i​t)/(1−i​t)x=(1+it)/(1-it) with t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R} we see that (6) is equivalent to

Set Ay:=L​[z​fy+y¯​z]​(0)A_{y}:=L\left[\frac{zf}{y+\overline{y}z}\right](0) and By:=L​[fy+y¯​z]​(0)B_{y}:=L\left[\frac{f}{y+\overline{y}z}\right](0). The assertion then follows from (54) and Lemma 38, since by (7) there is a y∈𝕋y\in\mathbb{T} such that
